title: Check the number claim
scenario: A draft analytics summary, mostly written by an AI assistant, contains this line: “Customer churn improved from 4.2% to 3.8% — a 12% reduction in churn.” The number is going into a board slide.
task: What is the right first move?

options.text: Trust it — churn figures were supplied by the analytics tool, so the percentage must be right.
options.feedback: The raw numbers may be right while the derived percentage is wrong — the arithmetic step is exactly where drafts slip. The source of the raw data says nothing about the calculation built on top of it.

options.text: Recompute the relative change from the raw numbers: 0.4 ÷ 4.2 is about 9.5%, not 12% — then restate the figure with both forms: down 0.4 points, or ~9.5% relative.
options.feedback: Extract, recompute, fix, and show both units. The absolute form (−0.4 points) survives scrutiny; the wrong relative figure would have been the slide's most quoted number.

options.text: Delete the percentage and keep only the raw numbers to be safe.
options.feedback: Safer, but you lose information the audience needs. The disciplined route is to recompute the percentage, not to abandon derived figures — churn reduction is genuinely useful when it is correct and unit-labelled.

options.text: Ask the AI to double-check its own calculation.
options.feedback: Asking the model that made the error to grade its own arithmetic is a coin flip with extra steps. The recompute is two seconds of your own work — do it yourself.

hints: The raw numbers can be right while the percentage derived from them is wrong — check the derivation, not just the source.
Absolute change and relative change are two different figures: 4.2 → 3.8 is a 0.4-point move, which is a certain percentage of the starting value.
explanation: “4.2% to 3.8%” is an absolute drop of 0.4 percentage points; as a relative change it is 0.4 ÷ 4.2 ≈ 9.5% — not the claimed 12%. Nothing looks wrong: the format is right, the direction is right, and it is off by a quarter. Derived figures (rates, totals, growth) are where AI drafts fail most plausibly, so they get recomputed before they ship — especially the one destined for a board slide, where the number will be quoted without its context.
